title: Say her name from across the room
step: Level 2, the distance version of the name check-in
note: Used by two steps. Drawn deliberately WITHOUT a leash: at this distance a taut line reads as pulling her in, and a slack one is an unreadable puddle of black across the floor. The whole point of the step is that she turns on her own. Say so if you'd rather it carried one. The bed is called out as a mattress on purpose: docs/pilot-prompts.md logs this exact key as drawing it too thin, shipped knowingly at 1.52.0. Round 5 passed every content claim and still failed: the 21:9 program hero cut the top of the handler's head and the square clipped her trailing arm. Her head sat at 15.6% of the frame height against a 21.5% band, and her arm at 10% of the width against a 12.5% one. The bands are not a matter of taste — they are cropBox() in renditions.mjs, measured: program-21x9 keeps 21.5%–78.6% of the height, square keeps 12.5%–87.5% of the width. A wide two-shot drifts out of both unless the scene text says so, because the master looks correct. Round 6 answered the safe-area percentages by translating both figures upward instead of reframing, so her head landed at 19.5% against a 21.5% band — still clipped — and the empty floor along the bottom grew rather than shrank. Stating a safe area invites that move; stating where the head and feet land does not, which is why round 7 gives the camera instead. Round 6 also drew the door with a four-pane window, following the live brief, which says four-pane in two places. The three redrawn interior closed-door scenes beside this one — 01-setup, 02-self and 03-name — all draw two. The brief is the drift's source and fixing it there means bumping BRIEF_ID and reconciling the whole set, so the window is pinned per-scene here instead and the brief is deliberately left alone. Round 7 fixed the window and the square and still clipped the 21:9, and measuring it settled why: the handler was drawn 632px tall (y193–y825) against a 621px band (rows 233–854). She was taller than the crop, so no offset and no focusY could contain her — shifting the band down to catch her head would have cut her feet. Placement was never the lever; size is. Rounds 5–7 all failed this way. The two-pane pin written here has since been reversed. The set was split 3–3 on the window and four panes won: it is what the live brief says in two places and what is physically true, since it is one door seen from either side. This picture, 01-setup, 02-self and 03-name were the four two-pane ones and all four were redrawn.
scene: The same entry hall, seen wider and from further back so there is real distance between the two figures. Lucy sits on her cool-grey dog bed on the right — a proper mattress with real thickness, a visibly padded slab a hand deep with a soft raised edge, not a flat mat or a thin rug, near the closed charcoal front door, and has turned her head back over her shoulder to look at the handler — her body stays square on the bed, only her head and ears have turned. The handler stands well off to the left, a clear span of empty floor between them, turned toward Lucy with one hand held open at her side in a small welcoming gesture. She is upright and relaxed, not crouching, not leaning, not patting her leg. No leash anywhere in this image — not on Lucy, not in the handler's hand, not on the floor. From the second reference take only the dog bed's shape, depth and cool grey; do not take the open door, the guest, or that image's camera distance. The door stays closed and nobody else is present. Background: the lavender wall, one baseboard line, the closed door, the doormat, the bed. Generous empty floor between them. Nothing else. THE DOOR'S WINDOW: a FOUR-PANE grid in the upper half of the door — two panes across and two panes down, divided by one vertical bar and one horizontal bar, pale spruce foliage beyond. Match attachment 1 exactly on this — it is the same door in the same hall, and it is four panes in every picture. HOW BIG THE HANDLER IS DRAWN: this is the measurement that matters most. From the top of her head to the soles of her shoes she must occupy no more than HALF the height of the picture — about 540 pixels of the 1086-pixel frame. She is a standing figure seen from across a room, not a near figure: draw her small. Above her head leave roughly a fifth of the frame as empty lavender wall, and below her feet roughly a quarter as floor. Lucy and her bed sit lower and to the right, the base of the bed no lower than four fifths of the way down. Keep the handler in from the left edge by about a tenth of the picture's width. Shot straight on from standing eye level.
mustBeTrue: Lucy stays sitting on the bed and has only turned her head toward the handler, the handler is clearly far away across the room and standing upright rather than crouching or beckoning with both arms, there is no leash anywhere in the picture, the bed is a thick padded mattress rather than a flat mat, the door's window is a four-pane grid — two across and two down, and the handler is drawn no more than half the frame tall with clear wall above her head and floor below her feet.
